tagline: Switchbacks climb Pine Creek Canyon to a tunnel inside its rock wall
intro: SR 9 climbs past mesas and follows the Virgin River into Zion before switchbacks lift it into Pine Creek Canyon and the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel. The whole highway is the Zion Park Scenic Byway; its SR 17–East Rim Trail Road section received national scenic designation in 2021. Utah’s tourism office highlights the national byway’s scenery, communities and public-land recreation, while UDOT advises allowing at least an hour and a half.

The eastern road made a regional park journey possible. After considering alternatives, the National Park Service chose Pine Creek, a route requiring a tunnel through the Great Arch. Work began in 1927 and finished in 1930, creating a road that joined a touring loop through Zion, Bryce Canyon, Cedar Breaks and the Grand Canyon’s North Rim. The Bureau of Public Roads handled the detailed road design, while the Park Service designed bridges, retaining walls and culverts under Thomas Chalmers Vint.

From I-15, drive through Hurricane and La Verkin, then east through Virgin, Rockville and Springdale. Inside the park, the road follows the North Fork of the Virgin River before turning up Pine Creek. Beyond the tunnel, continue past Checkerboard Mesa and out the east entrance to US 89 at Mount Carmel Junction.

moments.title: Grafton
moments.text: Grafton’s farming history includes the work of repeatedly clearing its irrigation ditches. The settlement began in 1859 as Wheeler, part of Brigham Young’s southern Utah cotton-growing project. The Virgin River flood of 1862 largely destroyed Wheeler, and settlers rebuilt upriver as New Grafton. Silt clogged the irrigation channels, and continued severe flooding discouraged resettlement. The Grafton Heritage Partnership formed in 1997 to preserve the townsite; restoration work included the old church and several houses. Residents had dug canals and planted orchards, some of which survive; the preservation partnership also bought farmland where agriculture continues.

moments.title: Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel
moments.text: The tunnel follows the canyon wall, keeping its centerline 21 feet from the outer rock face. Its galleries let in light and air, but also served construction: crews dumped excavated rock through them into the canyon. Workers used mining techniques, beginning inside the rock and working outward toward the portals. The Nevada Construction Company began the tunnel in 1927 and completed it in 1930. Parking spaces once provided at the galleries were removed for safety. The western portal has a cut-sandstone facade; the eastern opening is shaped to resemble a natural hole and is entered directly from a bridge.

moments.title: Checkerboard Mesa
moments.text: Two different processes drew the grid on Checkerboard Mesa’s white sandstone. The horizontal lines preserve cross-bedding from ancient dunes. Vertical and near-vertical lines developed as temperature changes, freezing and thawing, and wetting and drying made the sandstone expand and contract. The mesa rises 900 feet above the Zion-Mount Carmel Highway, immediately southwest of the east entrance. The name became official in 1935, after park superintendent Preston P. Patraw had called it Checkerboard Mountain. Crazy Quilt Mesa lies half a mile west, across a canyon whose rainwater pools provide water for resident bighorn sheep.
moments.notice: Horizontal dune bedding crosses vertical weathering lines in the white sandstone.

practical: Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel: The park entrance fee applies even to through traffic. Bicycles are prohibited in the Zion-Mount Carmel Tunnel. (checked 2026-10-11)
